Generally speaking, we don't expect the iPhone 18 Pro to have major upgrades over the previous generation. In fact, if you're currently using an older iPhone, there are plenty of reasons to buy the iPhone 17 Pro before next week's new device launch.

Among the few upgrades we anticipate, the biggest one appears to be the addition of a variable aperture lens to the main camera. But in practice, will this actually make a noticeable difference...?

Variable aperture allows control over depth of field

One of the biggest differences between shooting with a DSLR or mirrorless camera and shooting with an iPhone is the ability to control depth of field (DOF).

With a traditional camera, a wide aperture can produce a shallow depth of field effect, most commonly used to separate the subject from the background. Portrait photos are the most typical example (which is also why Apple's simulated shallow depth of field feature is called "Portrait Mode").

Conversely, when shooting landscapes or cityscapes, a narrow aperture is typically used to ensure everything from the foreground to the background is sharp and clear.

So variable aperture is a basic feature of any traditional camera lens. iPhones, on the other hand, have always used fixed aperture lenses. (There are actually some ways to achieve shallow depth of field effects with an iPhone, which I'll write about separately after the new device launches, but these are exceptions rather than the norm.)

iPhone lens gains variable aperture

We expect this year to be the first time an iPhone features a variable aperture lens. It's still unclear whether this feature will be available on both iPhone 18 Pro models, or just the Pro Max. Regardless, it's expected to be limited to the main lens, not the ultra-wide or telephoto lenses.

This looks like big news. In theory, a variable aperture lens would give us control over depth of field. But in practice, we shouldn't get too excited about achieving the kind of effect shown in the large image above—the reason being precisely that some things won't change.

Bad news

The main limiting factor for iPhone isn't the lens aperture—it's already quite large—but the size of the image sensor. All else being equal, the larger the sensor, the shallower the depth of field you can achieve. Compared to DSLRs and mirrorless cameras, the iPhone's sensor is simply too small, and this won't change this year.

With the same sensor size and only a slightly larger aperture, based on the laws of physics, we shouldn't expect too much from the effect.

Potential good news

Despite this, there may still be hope. Fitting a mechanical variable aperture into an iPhone lens is by no means a simple engineering feat. Precisely because of the lens's small size, this design is both complex and relatively expensive.

The question we need to ask is: since the expected benefits are only marginal, why would Apple put in so much effort and expense to do this? If the actual effect is only the kind of negligible difference we've calculated, it really doesn't seem worth it.

This makes me wonder—if Apple really plans to make a big deal promoting this new feature—they must have other tricks up their sleeve.

One possibility that immediately comes to mind is that the optical upgrade might simply be used to mask a major improvement to Portrait Mode. While the simulated shallow depth of field effect gets better every year, there's still room for improvement, and perhaps it's an upgrade to the chip's AI processing power that allows Apple to create more natural-looking results?

If that's really the case, I believe few people would mind this so-called "trick"—variable aperture only brings minor benefits, while the real improvements actually come from software. For most people, what matters most is the final result. This is my best guess for now.

Do you have a better guess? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
